text: So there’s no need to worry if something went wrong from reducing my dosage? I don’t need to worry about reducing my dosage this time? Any need to worry about continuing to lower the dosage? Do you think there’s still no need to slow down or be cautious in the final round? Do I want to give up on my medication reduction plan? Any need to second-guess the plan to stop medication because of the two seizures? Qun Wan was in the middle of a heated call with his daughter, Bowen Wan, when the phone suddenly went silent. The conversation, in early February, had started like most of their regular check-ins, a ritual that had kept them connected after Bowen moved from their small village in China to the United States. But the mood soured when she admitted she had been cutting back on a seizure medication that kept her severe epilepsy under control. She told him she had been slicing her tablets into pieces with a pill cutter, allowing her to reduce her dose by one-fourth, Qun recalled. Listen to your doctor, he pleaded. Bowen, 31, shot back that doctors didn’t care how the drug’s side effects affected her. She felt that the drug made her speaking stilted and her thinking slow. Then, abruptly, she stopped talking. Thirty seconds passed, then a minute, then two. It was longer than seizures she’d had before, Qun thought. He waited anxiously, calling out her name over and over. Qun knew his daughter had at times tinkered with her medications because she didn’t like the side effects or thought they weren’t working. But why this drug? As far as he could tell, it seemed to be helping. When Bowen finally came to, they agreed to talk more, after she had gotten some sleep. Thank you for your patience while we verify access.
